blocks.text: Biodiversity and classification are fundamental concepts in biology that provide insight into the vast array of life forms on Earth and their evolutionary relationships. In this chapter, we will study the biodiversity, highlighting the variety of life at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels. We will also explore the principles and methods of biological classification, which scientists use to organize and categorize organisms.

According to the five-kingdom classification system, proposed by American ecologists Rebert Whittaker in 1969, all organisms were divided into five kingdoms i.e., Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia. According to this system, the kingdom Monera included prokaryotes while all the other four kingdoms included eukaryotes. In 1990, American microbiologist Carl Woese suggested that there are two separate groups of prokaryotes i.e., Archaea and Bacteria. On the basis, he classified living organisms into three domains i.e., domain Archaea, domain Bacteria and domain Eukarya. According to his three-domain system, domain Archaea and domain Bacteria contain prokaryotes but they differ in a number of features.
The evolutionary relationship among organisms is called phylogeny. The diagram to show phylogeny, is called phylogenetic or evolutionary tree.

blocks.alt: Evolutionary tree of the three domains. A single trunk from the Common Ancestor splits in two: one branch leads to Domain Bacteria, drawn as a green cluster of many radiating lineages; the other divides again into Domain Archaea, a yellow cluster of lineages, and Domain Eukarya, a blue cluster of lineages.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.1: Evolutionary tree of the three domains (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The name is printed “Rebert”; the American ecologist who proposed the five-kingdom system in 1969 is Robert Whittaker.

Now biologists believe that Archaea and Bacteria evolved independently from some common ancestor. Molecular evidence suggests that archaea are more closely related to eukaryotes than to bacteria. In other words, Eukarya evolved from Archaea, after archaea split off from the Bacteria (Figure 1.1).
